reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: The contact quality is almost offensively good for a 22-year-old: 93.1 mph average exit velocity with a 51.5% hard-hit rate, and the expected numbers (.376 xwOBA, .510 xSLG) say the current production is underselling him. He's walking at 12.8% while striking out at only 18.6%, which is the discipline profile that keeps a middle-of-the-order bat from being pitched around into irrelevance. The whole thing hinges on whether Tampa can live with the defense — a 1st-percentile OAA at third is a real organizational problem, and if they can't, the profile changes shape before the bat ever gets a chance to carry it. If they do, you're looking at a 45-homer, .914 OPS season from a player who is still 22 years old.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The batting Statcast profile is essentially a closed argument: .409 xwOBA, 17.0% barrel rate, 14.3% walk rate — contact quality and plate discipline at the top of the sport simultaneously. A .926 OPS projection over 686 plate appearances fits the underlying numbers without needing to stretch them. On the mound the case is almost as clean, a 2.72 xERA built on a 98.1 mph fastball and a 30.4% whiff rate, with barrel rate allowed sitting at 3.8%, meaning hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact. The one genuine tension in this profile is durability: everything else resolves in his favor, and the whole read hinges on how many starts the Dodgers actually let him make.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .360 xwOBA and 47.4% hard-hit rate live in the same profile as a 34.7% chase rate and 26.1% K%, which is the whole tension here. He's running balls in play exceptionally hard, but a lot of contact is coming off pitches outside the zone, and when he misses he misses badly. The 11.7% walk rate softens the strikeout damage enough that a .361 OBP holds up in projection, and 29.6 ft/s sprint speed at the 96th percentile means every single and stolen base attempt plays up. If pitchers attack him more systematically off the plate and the chase rate climbs further, sustaining 31 home runs and an .855 OPS gets harder; if he tightens the zone even modestly, this is a near-premium offensive profile at a premium defensive position.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: A 2.76 xERA with a 5.6% walk rate is the profile of a legitimate frontline starter, not a guy running hot on sequencing luck. Skenes gets hitters out at a 29.7% strikeout clip while barely issuing free passes, and a 33.9% chase rate explains how: batters are expanding, chasing out of the zone rather than simply missing pitches over the plate. The projection, 3.25 ERA over 183.8 innings with 221 strikeouts, is a slight step back from what the Statcast profile says he's actually been, which means if the chase rate holds and the control stays sharp, that ERA could settle closer to the expected number than the projected one.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the exit velocity tell two completely different stories about the same swing. Walker's 93.9 mph average exit velocity sits at the 98th percentile, his xSLG is .506, and yet a 35.2% chase rate and 30.6% whiff rate are dragging his actual production below what the raw power deserves. The .368 xwOBA says the damage lands when he connects; the strikeout and chase numbers explain why he hasn't lived there consistently. If the plate discipline tightens even modestly, a .278/.341/.491 projection with 31 home runs and 20 steals starts to look conservative for a 23-year-old with that kind of exit velocity, and if it doesn't, you're left with a boom-or-bust middle-of-the-order profile that never quite settles into the numbers the batted-ball data keeps promising.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .306, 99th percentile, and the contact quality underneath it is what makes the .282 projection feel conservative rather than hopeful. At 92.9 mph average exit velocity and 52.2% hard-hit rate, he's doing elite contact damage, and the 30.3 ft/s sprint speed converts a portion of that damage that would retire anyone else. The one friction point is a 33.0% chase rate, which suppresses his walk opportunities and is the reason the OBP projection stays at .351 despite the raw contact ability; if that rate tightens even modestly, the offensive profile takes a significant step up. He's already a true shortstop, a 42-steal threat in projection, and a .819 OPS hitter — the question isn't whether he's good, it's how long before the chase discipline catches up to everything else he already is.

reports.name: CJ Abrams

At 36.1%, Abrams is expanding the zone at a rate that puts him in the bottom fifth of the league, and yet his .351 xwOBA and .468 xSLG say the contact itself is genuinely above-average quality when he does connect. The projection, .274/.346/.508 with 33 home runs and 26 steals across 662 plate appearances, reflects a hitter whose raw output can carry a lineup spot at shortstop even if the approach stays sloppy. reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Fourteen-point-six percent barrels with a 26.9% whiff rate is a quiet contradiction: the contact that finds the barrel is elite, but too much of the swing misses entirely. Stewart's xSLG sits at .474 while his xBA lands at .249, which is basically the profile in numbers — a power hitter who punishes mistakes and gets punished back by quality stuff. The 10.5% walk rate keeps the damage from compressing, and at 22 years old in Cincinnati, the projection landing at 31 home runs and a .792 OPS across a full 684 PA season is the floor if the whiff rate holds steady, and something meaningfully better if it doesn't.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.peak_summary: Projection: everyday regular with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 232 A PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile. Sixty-seven walks across A+ & A at 18 years old, an 18% BB% that translates to 12.3% at the MLB level while the average big-league hitter walks at 8.5%, and a .415 OBP that ranks 94th in the prospect pool — this is a teenager with a functional strike zone, not an accident. The power is where the ceiling question lives: a .204 ISO across A+ & A is genuine production for his age, but it translates to .136 at the MLB level, sitting below league average, which means the zone discipline has to carry the offensive identity if the pop doesn't grow. Thirty-nine stolen bases across A+ & A adds a dimension the translation can't capture, and if the hit tool firms up, the everyday regular ceiling is plausible on an accelerated timeline. If the contact slips under big-league velocity, what's left is a high-OBP utility shortstop, valuable, but a different conversation.

reports.name: Walker Jenkins
reports.peak_summary: Projection: low-end everyday regular with medium risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 196 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact is the calling card, and the swing-and-miss is almost nonexistent. Across AAA & A+ & A this season, Jenkins is striking out at just a 14% clip over 213 plate appearances, which translates to an 18.6% MLB-equivalent rate, well short of what most hitters post in the majors, and he's pairing that with 27 walks against only 30 strikeouts. The power, though, is where the conversation gets honest: a .19 ISO in the minors flattens to a .147 MLB-equivalent, nearly indistinguishable from the MLB mean of .150, which means if the game power doesn't develop beyond what's here, he becomes a high-contact, on-base-oriented center fielder who lives on the fringes of everyday status rather than holding it comfortably. A low-end everyday regular if the bat-to-ball skills carry and the power ticks forward; a useful bench piece if the contact stays but the power stalls exactly where it is.

reports.name: Cristopher Sánchez
reports.published_report: That 38.7% chase rate is the engine, 99th percentile, the kind of number that makes hitters expand the zone before they've decided to swing. Pair it with a 4.5% walk rate and a 32.4% whiff rate and you have a pitcher who manufactures swing-and-miss without losing the zone, which is the rarest combination a starting pitcher can carry. The contact he does allow comes in hard, 43.8% hard-hit rate, so the profile hinges entirely on hitters continuing to chase pitches they can't do damage on when they find them. If that chase rate erodes and hitters lay off long enough to wait for something they can drive, the hard contact becomes a real problem, but right now the sequencing keeps it dormant, and a 2.80 ERA projection over 205.3 innings reflects exactly that fragile-looking-but-functional balance.

His K% sits at 38.2 and his BB% at 4.6, both near the top of the distribution, and a 38.0% whiff rate says hitters aren't just missing — they're helpless. The hard-hit numbers are loud in the wrong direction: a 47.3% hard-hit rate and 91.5 mph average exit velo against him are among the ugliest marks you'll find, which tells you the 100.2 mph fastball gets punished when it does get hit, and the profile hinges entirely on whether he can keep the barrel rate at 4.1% while those exit velocities stay in the background. If the whiff rate holds, the hard contact looks like a quirk of who he faces rather than a structural flaw; if the swing-and-miss dips even modestly, those exit velocities stop being background noise.

reports.name: Theo Gillen
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 265 A+ PA.
reports.published_report: The .421 OBP and 35 stolen bases across AA & A+ are the two things pulling in opposite directions here, and that tension is worth sitting with. Theo Gillen is doing legitimate damage, .966 OPS, 15 home runs, 48 walks in 356 plate appearances, but the .398 BABIP is doing heavy lifting on that batting average, and the MLB translation peels the ISO back to .156 and bumps the strikeout rate to 26.2%, both of which narrow the ceiling considerably. The speed and on-base instincts are real enough to survive some contact regression; the power is the question, because if the ISO doesn't hold even close to its current shape against better pitching, what's left is a high-walk, high-speed profile that lands as a bench or platoon bat rather than an everyday center fielder. At 20, the runway is long, but the floor and ceiling land in the same neighborhood, which means this is a profile betting on refinement, not a breakout.

reports.name: Edward Cabrera
reports.published_report: The fastball sits 96.1 mph and hitters chase his stuff at a 32.6% rate, but when they do make contact, they absolutely punish it — 42.7% hard-hit rate, 11.8% barrel rate, average exit velocity of 91.3 mph. That contact profile is the whole problem. The chase is generating misses but not soft contact, which is the combination that produces a 4.87 xERA and leaves him projecting to 113.9 innings of 4.77 ERA ball with a 9.4% walk rate compounding the damage. If the stuff can't suppress barrels, the ceiling here is a back-end starter who eats innings on good days and gets blown up on bad ones.

reports.name: Michael Soroka
reports.published_report: The 5.1% walk rate is the load-bearing wall of this profile. Everything else about Soroka is average-to-middling on the Statcast card: a 23.7% strikeout rate, a 4.00 xERA that says the 3.52 ERA is getting some help, whiff rate in the bottom quarter of the league. But a walk rate that sits in the 93rd percentile buys time for everything else to play, and his 33.6% chase rate suggests hitters are chasing rather than simply missing, which keeps the low-walk number from looking accidental. The 2516 rpm fastball spin is legitimately loud even if the 93.7 mph velocity isn't, and that combination, not the ERA, is the argument for why 130.4 innings at roughly this level is plausible rather than optimistic. If the chase rate slips and the strikeout rate falls with it, a fastball that soft with a middling whiff rate leaves him pitching to contact and leaning hard on a defense that has to show up every night.

His calling card is barrel suppression, holding hitters to a 6.0% barrel rate, but he gets there with a 92.6 mph fastball that generates a 22.5% whiff rate — soft contact allowed, not swing-and-miss earned. The strikeout rate at 19.7% is the vulnerability; if opposing lineups stop chasing and start working counts, that contact-management profile thins out fast. What he probably is: a back-of-rotation starter who logs serious innings, keeps the walks manageable at 7.2%, and gives Atlanta a steady if unexciting rotation piece rather than anything they can rely on in October.

reports.name: Caleb Durbin
reports.published_report: The contact skills are not the problem. A 15.2% whiff rate and 13.3% strikeout rate sit in the top tier of the league, and he puts the ball in play consistently enough that the bat-to-ball piece is genuinely repeatable. The problem is what happens when he does make contact: 84.5 mph average exit velocity and a 2.6% barrel rate produce an xSLG of .329, which is where power profiles go to die. ValuCast's projection splits the difference between the discipline and the soft contact, landing on .245/.310/.399 with 15 home runs across 558 plate appearances, which reads like a second-division regular if the speed (19 projected steals) and glove (87th-percentile OAA) carry their weight. He becomes a useful everyday third baseman if the contact volume papers over the exit velocity floor; strip out the speed contribution and you're looking at a bat that's too passive to drive runs and not quite patient enough at 6.6% walk rate to manufacture them another way.

The contact side holds up reasonably well, a 19.2% whiff rate and a .254 xBA both landing near average, but a 43.7% chase rate explains why pitchers can afford to attack him and why that walk rate isn't noise. A 12.7% walk rate paired with a 16.2% strikeout rate is a genuinely elite zone-management combination, and an .xBA of .278 at the 86th percentile says the contact itself plays up even when the exit velocity, sitting at 89.1 mph, looks ordinary. The 6.3% barrel rate and 37.1% hard-hit rate are below-average, which means the 20-homer projection leans on volume and an above-average hit tool rather than a true power profile. reports.name: Kahlil Watson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 259 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The power is loud for a center fielder who spent years looking like a bat-speed dart with no thump: 12 home runs and a .230 ISO at AAA are not what you expected from Watson. Thirty-seven walks in 259 plate appearances translate to an 11.1% MLB-equivalent walk rate, and the on-base work at .363 reflects that patience showing up in the actual line. The problem sitting in the middle of this profile is a 29% strikeout rate that translates to 27.4% in MLB context, well clear of the 22.0% MLB average, and a .249 average propped up by a .321 BABIP that probably softens when the level goes up. If the power holds shape and the strikeouts plateau, you get a bench bat with genuine pop and enough patience to be useful; if the average erodes further under big-league velocity, the floor is a depth outfielder who never quite sticks.

reports.published_report:
The fastball at 97.7 mph is elite. Everything around it, right now, is not.

His Statcast profile is a study in contradiction: a 28.6% whiff rate that says hitters are genuinely fooled, alongside a 12.0% barrel rate and 44.8% hard-hit rate that say when they do connect, it's damage. The 9.1% walk rate bleeds into the contact damage, which is why the xERA lands at 4.59 despite the swing-and-miss. If he tightens the zone and the barrel rate normalizes, the fastball's upside is real enough to profile as a mid-rotation starter; if the command and contact suppression stay where they are, he's a limited-inning arm fighting to reach 134.7 projected innings at 4.73.

reports.name: Kyle Karros
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the foundation here. At 12.8%, Karros draws free passes at a rate that puts him well ahead of most hitters in baseball, and it's why a .341 xwOBA sits comfortably above what his exit velocity would suggest on its own. The contact quality is quietly honest, 89.7 mph average exit velo, 43.3% hard-hit rate, nothing that screams impact but nothing broken either, and the 24.4% chase rate explains how he keeps getting to favorable counts despite swing-and-miss rates that are right around league average. The projection's .356 OBP across 487 PA is the most credible part of the line; the 12 home runs are fine for a third baseman who profiles as a solid regular rather than a middle-of-the-order force, and that ceiling shrinks fast if Coors Field ever flatters his raw numbers in ways the xSLG at .408 doesn't actually support.

reports.name: Spencer Torkelson
reports.published_report: The case for Torkelson rests on one uncomfortable split: a 14.6% barrel rate sitting at the 90th percentile while a 32.8% strikeout rate sits at the 2nd. He makes genuine hard contact when he connects, walks at a solid 10.8% clip, and chases at just 23.1%, which is elite plate discipline by chase-rate standards. But a 31.6% whiff rate means pitchers are winning inside the zone, and an .xBA of .213 tells you the contact that isn't barreled is mostly outs. If he can cut the swing-and-miss without sacrificing the barrel rate, the projection's .418 SLG and 28 home runs are a floor rather than a ceiling; if he can't, the .211 AVG is the story and first base is an unforgiving place to hide it.

reports.name: Will Warren
reports.published_report: The fastball spin is doing a lot of heavy lifting. At 2538 rpm, Warren sits in the 91st percentile there, but the rest of the Statcast profile tells a quieter story: a 22.3% whiff rate and 28.3% chase rate that both land below average, a 4.49 xERA that the projection's 4.06 ERA is outrunning. The spin hasn't yet converted into swing-and-miss volume, and until it does, the ceiling here is roughly what the projection describes: a back-end starter who eats innings, collects nine quality starts, and doesn't beat himself with walks at 7.9%. If the whiff rate climbs toward something that matches what the spin theoretically allows, he becomes a genuine rotation piece; if it doesn't, he's a depth starter whose ERA will drift back toward the xERA.

If it doesn't, he's a patient bench bat who makes pitchers work and not much else.

report_llm.text: The translation is the problem. Eleven home runs and a .169 ISO at AAA look like a power hitter developing; at MLB-equivalent, that ISO drops to .141, below the .150 MLB average, which is the wrong direction for a corner infield profile that needs the bat to carry it. The contact is genuinely encouraging, 60 strikeouts across 329 AAA plate appearances translating to a 20.5% clip where the typical big-leaguer strikes out at 22.0%, and that is a real skill. But the walk rate doesn't suggest a patient masher, it suggests a hitter who makes contact and not much else, and a first baseman living on contact without lifting the ISO is a roster bubble problem waiting to happen. Everything hinges on whether the raw power grows into the ISO gap, because if it doesn't, the ceiling stays bench and ValuCast's +16 move over three days tells you more about thin corner depth leaguewide than it does about this profile.

reports.name: Jack Mahoney
reports.peak_summary: Projection: multi-inning or setup reliever with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 62 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The 2.00 ERA over 62 innings at AA is the loudest number in this profile, and the translation is where it gets complicated. Mahoney's strikeout rate doesn't carry well to the majors: his 8.4 K/9 at AA translates to 7.7, a tick below a league-average 8.6, and his walk rate, clean-looking at 3.0 BB/9 in Double-A, translates to essentially the same as a league-average MLB arm. What that means is the run prevention has to come from somewhere other than missing bats, and if it doesn't travel with him, what's left is a reliever profile: the floor is depth, the ceiling is multi-inning or setup work, and the profile hinges entirely on whether the weak contact or sequencing suppressing that ERA is repeatable under better competition. He's risen +15 in ValuCast's rankings over a three-day stretch, which reflects the ERA's gravity, but the translation argues for patience before letting it change your evaluation.

reports.name: Nate Furman
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 413 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the whole argument. If a second baseman can reach base at a tick above average and swipe bags (17 stolen bases this season), he has a bench job; if the .283 average softens even modestly against better pitching, the profile thins to a depth piece. Ceiling and floor land close together here, both pointing toward bench or platoon bat.

reports.name: Trent Grisham
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile keeps screaming that Grisham should hit more than he does: a .353 xwOBA with 91.2 mph average exit velocity and a 16.4% strikeout rate that most outfielders would trade anything for. The gap between those underlying numbers and a projected .225 average lives almost entirely in his sprint speed, 26.7 ft/s, which turns sharply-hit grounders into outs that a faster player beats out. His 13.7% walk rate is elite-tier discipline, and when you pair that with a 16.9% chase rate sitting at the very top of the leaderboard, you have a hitter who genuinely controls the zone, he just can't outrun the shift or leg out singles anymore. If the .413 projected SLG starts to look more like his .451 xSLG, this is a solid everyday corner outfielder; if the average stays buried near .225, he's a counting-stats disappointment despite skills that deserve better.

His xERA sits at 3.83 and his xwOBA at .303, both comfortably better than a league-average starter, yet ValuCast projects a 4.63 ERA over 172.5 innings — the difference lives almost entirely in his walk rate. A 9.3% BB% is the anchor dragging him; the whiff rate at 26.6% is fine, but hitters don't need to chase him at 28.8% because he'll eventually come to them. What saves contact when it does happen is genuine: 2423 rpm on the fastball and a 5.4% barrel rate suggest the stuff plays up in quality even if the command doesn't hold the zone, and 87.8 mph average exit velocity reflects that. If the walk rate tightens even modestly, the underlying contact profile points toward a mid-rotation arm; if it stays where it is, that 4.63 ERA is about right for what he delivers.

reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 139 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The .391 BABIP is the first thing to squint at, and it's also the first thing that could make this whole read moot. That strikeout rate translates to 27%, well above the 22% MLB baseline, and at a contact floor that shaky, the ISO needs to hold to keep the profile interesting. If the BABIP normalizes and the strikeouts stay, what's left is a bench outfielder with some speed and fringe power, not nothing, but not a regular.

reports.name: Tekoah Roby
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with high risk. The current pitching shape is mixed over 47 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The control is what makes this profile worth a second look. Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.
